headline.statement: The one comparison in Table 2 that favours placebo is significant at the table's own stated threshold but is the only significant comparison left unmarked, while both significant comparisons favouring Cerebrolysin carry asterisks.
headline.evidence: Table 2 footnote: "* p < 0.05 compared with the placebo group." Table 2, ΔFMA-LL, T0–T1: Cerebrolysin "3.3 ± 5.0" (n = 59) vs Placebo "5.6 ± 6.0" (n = 51), no asterisk. Recomputed from those printed values, the entire achievable p-interval is [0.0229, 0.0429] — below 0.05 under Welch (p = 0.0329) and Student (p = 0.0305) and across the full rounding box of the printed means and SDs. The two starred cells are ΔFMA-T T1–T2 (achievable p [0.0136, 0.0201]) and ΔFMA-UL T1–T2 (achievable p [0.0198, 0.0303]) — both favouring Cerebrolysin. The six genuinely non-significant cells recompute at p = 0.12 to 0.75; e.g. ΔFMA-T T0–T1 achievable p [0.261, 0.308].
headline.plain: The table marks with a star every treatment-versus-placebo comparison that reached statistical significance. Three of the nine comparisons actually reach it. The two where the drug did better are starred; the one where placebo did better — lower-limb recovery during the three-week treatment period — is not, even though recalculating it from the numbers printed in the same row gives a result comfortably past the table's own cutoff. A reader of the table would not see that placebo outperformed the drug on that measure.

findings.title: Adverse-event percentages irreconcilable with the stated safety population of 119
findings.reported: "Of all patients treated with the studied medication (n = 119), a total of 92.4% received 21 infusions (Cerebrolysin 96.7%, placebo 87.9%). Although five patients in the Cerebrolysin group (8.1%) and five in the placebo group (8.3%) suffered from an adverse event..."
findings.computed: Sweeping every denominator from 2 to the paper's own stated safety population of 119: 96.7% is attainable only at n ∈ {30, 60, 61, 90, 91, 92} and 8.1% only at n ∈ {37, 62, 74, 86, 99, 111} — the intersection is empty. Same for the placebo arm: 87.9% at n ∈ {33, 58, 66, 91, 99, 107, 116}, 8.3% at n ∈ {12, 24, 36, 48, 60, 72, 84, 96, 108, 109} — intersection empty. The infusion figures resolve to 59/61 and 51/58, summing to 61 + 58 = 119, the treated population. The adverse-event figures resolve to 5/62 and 5/60, summing to 122, the randomized population.
findings.assumptions: n_max = 119 is the paper's own stated safety population, not a bound supplied by this review, so the empty intersection is a fact about the paper's numbers. Assumes both percentages in these two adjacent sentences are shares of the population the first sentence names, which is what the text asserts.

consequence.explanation: Bears on the Conclusions claim that the regimen "was safe and well-tolerated", since the adverse-event rates are computed on a denominator other than the safety population the paper defines.

findings.plain: The paper says 119 patients received the drug or placebo, and gives percentages for how many completed all infusions and how many had a side effect. Those two sets of percentages cannot both be shares of 119 — the completion figures point to arm sizes of 61 and 58 (adding to 119, the treated patients), while the side-effect figures point to 62 and 60 (adding to 122, the patients originally assigned). The likeliest explanation is that side-effect rates were worked out on everyone randomised rather than on everyone treated. The substance of the safety claim is unchanged — five events in each arm either way — but the rates as printed are not the rates for the group the sentence names.

findings.title: Placebo denominator of 52 in the MEP result, against a placebo arm of 51 everywhere else
findings.reported: "The MEP response rates were significantly increased at T2 in both groups (p < 0.05); 42.4% (25 out of 59 patients) in the Cerebrolysin group and 35.3% (18 out of 52 patients) in the placebo group."
findings.computed: The triple (18, 52, 35.3%) cannot cohere: 18/52 = 34.6% and 19/52 = 36.5%, so 35.3% is unattainable on a denominator of 52. R's `scrutiny` package independently returns inconsistent for the equivalent proportion 0.353 at n = 52, agreeing with our engine. The adjacent Cerebrolysin figure 25/59 = 42.4% is correct, as are the T1 figures 20/59 = 33.9% and 14/51 = 27.5%.
findings.assumptions: The cross-check was run as GRIM on the proportion 0.353 at 3 decimals, which is the same question as 35.3% at 1 decimal. The paper's placebo full analysis set is stated as n = 51 in the abstract, Results 3.1 and the Table 1 column header; 18/51 = 35.294%, which rounds to exactly 35.3%.

consequence.explanation: A descriptive sentence; no significance claim in the paper depends on whether the placebo denominator reads 51 or 52.

findings.plain: One sentence says 18 of 52 placebo patients is 35.3 percent. It is not — 18 out of 52 is 34.6 percent. But 18 out of 51 is 35.3 percent exactly, and 51 is the placebo group size the paper uses everywhere else. This is almost certainly a mistyped number in a single sentence rather than anything about the data, and nothing the paper concludes rests on it. It is recorded because the printed figures do not add up as written.

findings.title: Significant lower-limb difference favouring placebo left unstarred in Table 2
findings.location: Table 2, ΔFMA-LL row, T0–T1 column, against the table footnote
findings.reported: Footnote: "* p < 0.05 compared with the placebo group." The cell "3.3 ± 5.0" (Cerebrolysin, n = 59) against "5.6 ± 6.0" (Placebo, n = 51) carries no asterisk, implying p ≥ 0.05.
findings.computed: Achievable p-interval [0.0229, 0.0429] across both Welch and Student readings and the full rounding box of the printed one-decimal means and SDs; point estimates p = 0.0329 (Welch) and p = 0.0305 (Student). The whole interval lies below 0.05. By contrast the starred ΔFMA-UL T1–T2 cell has achievable p [0.0198, 0.0303] — overlapping this cell's interval — so no single threshold both stars that cell and leaves this one unstarred. The six correctly unstarred cells recompute far from the threshold (ΔFMA-T T0–T1 achievable p [0.261, 0.308]).
findings.assumptions: The paper states only that "the independent t-test was used between the two groups to analyze the change in motor function" and does not name Welch or Student; both were computed and both give p < 0.05. The likeliest benign explanation, stated here rather than in a footnote: the authors may have run only the T1–T2 comparisons they discuss in the text and starred those, in which case the footnote over-promises by implying every cell was tested. The paper never claims in prose that lower-limb T0–T1 was non-significant.

consequence.explanation: A significant between-group difference in lower-limb recovery during the treatment period, favouring placebo by 5.6 to 3.3 points, is invisible in a table whose two marked results both favour Cerebrolysin.

findings.plain: Table 2 uses a star to mark every drug-versus-placebo comparison that passed the usual statistical cutoff. Three comparisons pass it. Both that favour the drug are starred; the one that favours placebo — lower-limb recovery over the three weeks of treatment, where placebo patients gained 5.6 points against 3.3 — is not. Recalculating from the numbers printed in that very row puts it past the cutoff under every standard way of doing the test. The most likely innocent explanation is that the authors only ran the comparisons they discuss in the text, but as the table stands a reader cannot see that placebo won on this measure.

findings.title: Four baseline variables leaning consistently in Cerebrolysin's favour, reported as "no significant differences"
findings.reported: "There were no significant differences in demographic and clinical characteristics between the two groups, including initial stroke severity measured by NIHSS, motor impairments, and lesion volume." Table 1: FMA-T 26.2 ± 13.6 vs 21.6 ± 13.7 (p = 0.085); FMA-LL 13.4 ± 7.4 vs 11.0 ± 7.4 (p = 0.097); Stroke side 21:38 vs 26:25 (p = 0.104); Lesion volume 43.9 ± 66.7 vs 69.9 ± 90.5 cm³ (p = 0.117).
findings.computed: The ten baseline p-values are 0.585, 0.246, 0.104, 0.882, 0.618, 0.085, 0.220, 0.097, 0.117, 0.817. Four cluster between 0.085 and 0.117 and every one of them favours the Cerebrolysin arm prognostically: less baseline motor impairment (4.6 FMA-T points, a 21% relative advantage) and 26 cm³ smaller mean lesions (a 37% relative advantage). No covariate adjustment is reported for any analysis. The omnibus baseline-similarity tests were correctly refused by the tooling because the trial states block randomisation stratified by clinical centre, which forces balance by construction; and because Table 1's motor rows are mutually predictive by definition (FMA-T = FMA-UL + FMA-LL), which violates the independence those tests assume. There is no suspicious uniformity here — the spread leans the other way, toward imbalance.
findings.assumptions: None beyond the paper's own printed values. This is a directional observation about the magnitude and sign of the imbalances, not an omnibus test; no baseline-similarity test was run, and none should be on a stratified design.

consequence.explanation: The paper's own Discussion states that "the strongest predictor of motor outcome at 3 months in stroke patients is motor function in the acute phase", yet the treatment arm began less impaired on that predictor and no analysis adjusts for it.

findings.plain: Randomised trials expect some chance differences between groups at the start. Here four such differences all point the same way: the Cerebrolysin patients started with better motor scores and smaller strokes than the placebo patients. None reaches statistical significance individually, and the paper reports simply that there were no significant differences. But the paper itself says that starting motor function is the single strongest predictor of how much a patient recovers, and no analysis adjusts for the head start. This does not mean the result is wrong; it means part of the drug group's better outcome could reflect who ended up in it.

findings.title: Three of seven continuous baseline p-values not reproducible as independent t-tests, with no test named
findings.location: Table 1, Age / NIHSS / Lesion volume rows, against Section 2.5
findings.computed: Given the printed means, SDs and group sizes, the achievable two-tailed p under an independent t-test is [0.2484, 0.2967] for age (reported 0.246), [0.8935, 1.0] for NIHSS (reported 0.882), and [0.0852, 0.0954] for lesion volume (reported 0.117). All three reported values sit just outside their achievable intervals. The lesion-volume gap is the largest. Separately, a normal distribution with mean 43.9 and SD 66.7 would place 25.5% of patients below zero volume, which is impossible for a volume — so the blanket claim that "all assessment values were found to have a normal distribution" is hard to sustain for this variable, though the tool notes correctly that a parametric test requires normality of the sampling distribution of the mean, not of the raw values.
findings.assumptions: Downgraded from the sweep tool's `highly_suspicious`, because the independent-t reading is an assumption this review supplied: the paper never states which test produced Table 1's p-values. NIHSS is a bounded ordinal score and lesion volume is strongly right-skewed (SD 1.5× the mean, bounded below by zero); a rank-based test is the natural choice for both and would legitimately give different p-values. The four remaining continuous rows — MMSE, FMA-T, FMA-UL, FMA-LL — do reproduce cleanly as independent t-tests.

consequence.explanation: Supports the baseline-balance claim; under a t-test reading the lesion-volume p would be nearer 0.09 than 0.117, still non-significant but closer to the threshold, which matters given the 26 cm³ raw difference.

findings.plain: For three of the ten baseline rows — age, stroke severity and lesion size — the reported p-value does not match what an ordinary two-group comparison of the printed averages would give. The most likely reason is benign: the paper never says which statistical test it used for this table, and for skewed measurements like lesion size a different, equally standard test is the normal choice and would give a different number. The other four rows of this type match exactly. Worth asking the authors which test was used, rather than treating as an error.

findings.title: Screening total two patients short of the randomised and excluded counts
findings.reported: "A total of 174 stroke patients were screened. Of these, 122 patients were randomized after excluding 54 patients who did not meet criteria of severe motor impairment (30 patients) or who refused to participate (24 patients)."
findings.computed: 122 + 54 = 176, exceeding the stated 174 by 2. The exclusion reasons themselves reconcile exactly (30 + 24 = 54), and every downstream stage reconciles exactly: 122 − 3 = 119 treated, 119 − 9 = 110 full analysis set, 59 + 51 = 110, 21 + 19 = 40 and 38 + 32 = 70 summing to 110, 102 − 10 = 92 for DTI, 92 − 11 = 81 for rs-fMRI. This was the single inconsistent row out of 33 sums evaluated across the paper.
findings.assumptions: Tolerance zero, as these are exact patient counts. None beyond the paper's own statements.

consequence.explanation: No analysis uses the screened total; the analysed samples all reconcile internally.

findings.plain: The paper says 174 patients were screened, of whom 122 were randomised after 54 were excluded — but 122 plus 54 is 176, not 174. Either the screening figure should read 176, or two patients are unaccounted for. Every other count in the participant flow adds up exactly, so this is isolated to one sentence and does not affect any analysis.

findings.title: Manuscript defects in Methods and back matter: wrong imaging timepoints, duplicated registry number, repeated data statement
findings.reported: Section 2.5: "The paired t-test was performed to analyze significant changes from T2 to T1 in participants' imaging measures within groups." Section 2.1: "Inclusion and exclusion criteria for the second trial (NCT02768571) were the same as those used in the first trial (NCT02768571)." The Data Availability Statement appears twice, verbatim, separated by the Conflicts of Interest section.
findings.computed: Imaging was acquired only at two timepoints — Section 2.1 states "Changes in the neuroplasticity of the motor network were assessed by diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) and resting state functional magnetic resonance imaging (rs-fMRI) at T0 and T2" — and Table 3 accordingly reports T0 versus T2. There is no T1 imaging, so the Methods name a comparison that cannot have been run. The registration sentence gives the identifier NCT02768571 for both the second and the first trial; the paper states two paragraphs earlier that the trials are NCT01996761 and NCT02768571, so the second instance should evidently read NCT01996761.
findings.assumptions: None beyond the paper's own statements; these are textual contradictions, not arithmetic.

consequence.explanation: The registry error sits in the sentence that establishes which trial's eligibility criteria — including the FMA-T 0–49 entry restriction defining the study population — the pooled dataset was built on.

findings.plain: Three proofreading problems. The statistical methods describe comparing brain scans between two timepoints that were never both scanned; the actual analysis compares the right ones, so this is a description error rather than an analysis error. The sentence explaining which trial's entry rules were used gives the same registration number twice, so it is unclear which trial is meant. And the data-availability paragraph is printed twice. Individually trivial, but they show the manuscript was not closely checked, which is relevant context for the numerical slips found elsewhere.

findings.title: Title claim of prevented degeneration against Table 3, where both arms degenerate significantly
findings.reported: Title: "Cerebrolysin Combined with Rehabilitation Enhances Motor Recovery and Prevents Neural Network Degeneration in Ischemic Stroke Patients with Severe Motor Deficits."
findings.computed: Table 3 reports a significant within-group decline from T0 to T2 in the Cerebrolysin arm on every one of the seven white-matter measures (all p < 0.001), alongside the same significant decline in placebo. Corticospinal tract, Cerebrolysin: 0.901 ± 0.070 falling to 0.816 ± 0.095, p < 0.001. The between-group interaction is significant (p = 0.0167), so the decline is slower under Cerebrolysin — but it is not prevented. The abstract states this accurately ("less degenerative changes"); the title does not.
findings.assumptions: None beyond the paper's own statements. The judgement concerns the word "prevents" against the paper's own within-group results.

consequence.explanation: The title asserts prevention of neural network degeneration; the paper's own data show significant degeneration in both arms, attenuated rather than prevented in the treatment arm.

findings.plain: The title says the drug prevents the brain's wiring from degenerating after a stroke. The paper's own table shows that wiring degraded significantly over three months in the drug group too — on every measure — just less than in the placebo group. The abstract describes this correctly as "less degenerative changes"; the title overstates it as prevention.

findings.title: No confidence interval reported anywhere in the paper
findings.reported: The paper reports p-values and two Cohen's d values, and states repeatedly that comparisons showed "no significant difference" — at baseline, in MEP response rate at T1 and T2, and for contralesional connectivity, interhemispheric connectivity and network efficiency.
findings.computed: No interval estimate appears for any comparison in any of the three tables or in the text. Consequently none of the paper's null claims could be tested against the largest effect its own data still permit: the tool for that check requires a confidence interval, and there is none to supply. Separately, no a-priori power or sample-size calculation is stated — only that "the sample size in our previous study was not large enough" — so nothing about the study's sensitivity can be reproduced either.
findings.assumptions: None beyond the paper's own statements. This is an observation about what the paper does and does not report.

consequence.explanation: Six or more "no significant difference" claims — baseline balance, MEP group differences at T1 and T2, and three imaging measures — cannot be distinguished from underpowered nulls without interval estimates.

findings.plain: The paper never gives a range of plausible values for any of its results, only whether each was statistically significant. That matters most for the several places where it says two groups did not differ: without a range, there is no way to tell whether the data show the groups are genuinely similar or simply that the study was too small to detect a difference. Reporting these ranges is standard for clinical trials.

findings.title: Bonferroni correction stated without a family or a threshold, and its effect on eight significant imaging results uncomputable
findings.reported: "To correct for multiple comparisons, the Bonferroni correction was used." Table 3 marks eight of eleven group-by-time interactions as significant, with raw p-values of 0.0091, 0.0167, 0.0185, 0.0256, 0.0263, 0.0280, 0.0305 and 0.0449. Table 2 presents nine between-group comparisons.
findings.computed: Nothing. The multiplicity tool returned n_tests = 0 on every attempt, in both the sweep and this review, with two different payload shapes — it did not parse the supplied tests. No multiplicity arithmetic has been substituted by hand. What can be said from the checks that did run: the paper never states which family the correction was applied to, nor at what threshold; the reported p-values in Table 3 are marked significant against 0.05, which is the uncorrected threshold; and no single threshold reproduces Table 2's pattern of asterisks (see the ΔFMA-LL finding).
findings.assumptions: The reproduction command below runs but returns n_tests = 0 rather than an analysis; it is given so a reader can confirm the tool failure rather than reproduce a result. The seven corpus-callosum and white-matter interactions plausibly form one family and the four connectivity measures another, but the paper does not say, and choosing the family is a judgement the tool cannot make.

consequence.explanation: Whether the eight significant imaging interactions that underpin the title's neuroprotection claim survive the correction the paper says it applied could not be determined.

findings.plain: The paper says it corrected for the fact that it ran many tests at once — a standard safeguard against false positives — but never says which group of tests it applied the correction to, or what cutoff resulted. Eight of the eleven brain-imaging results it calls significant have p-values between 0.009 and 0.045, which are the kind of borderline values most vulnerable to such a correction. The software needed to work out how many would survive failed to run, so this genuinely could not be settled either way, and no substitute calculation was made.

not_checked.reason: The flowchart is artwork and its internal box labels are absent from the PDF text layer; only the caption is extractable. This is the one place the per-arm randomised split (the 61/58 versus 62/60 question) would be printed, so the safety-denominator conflict cannot be resolved from the paper as extracted.

not_checked.location: Results 3.2, all eight simple linear regression results (r² = 0.534, 0.571, 0.125, 0.101, 0.504, 0.428, 0.571, 0.527 with their p-values)
not_checked.reason: No validated tool converts an r² plus n into a p-value; the regression checkers require a coefficient and standard error, which the paper does not report, and statcheck does not recognise this notation. Deriving F from r² by hand would be unvalidated arithmetic. Noted for the record: the placebo FMA-T model and the placebo FMA-UL model are both reported as r² = 0.571, an unusual coincidence between two different outcomes in the same group.

not_checked.location: Table 3, all 14 DTI within-group T0 versus T2 paired t-tests
not_checked.reason: Every p-value in this block is printed as the bound '<0.001' rather than an exact value. A bound only lower-bounds t, so the recovered pre-post correlation is itself a bound and no inconsistency can be established. A limit of the reporting, not a tool failure.

Every quantity is continuous by construction — proportional fractional anisotropy is a ratio of averaged voxel values, connectivity is a mean correlation, efficiency is a graph metric — so the granularity checks (GRIM, GRIMMER, SPRITE, DEBIT) are inapplicable and were withheld rather than misapplied.

not_checked.location: Table 1, all 16 mean ± SD and n (%) cells
not_checked.reason: Zero of sixteen cells were checkable by granularity methods, each refusal principled: NIHSS, MMSE, FMA-T, FMA-UL and FMA-LL are multi-item composites whose means move in steps of 1/(items × n) rather than 1/n, and age and lesion volume are continuous. The same refusal held for all 36 Table 2 checks, where change scores have no stated scale maximum.

not_checked.location: Results 3.2, the claim that MEP response rates 'significantly increased at T2 in both groups (p < 0.05)'
not_checked.reason: This is a within-subject comparison of a binary outcome requiring McNemar's test, which needs the discordant-pair counts. Only marginal totals are reported (13 to 25 in Cerebrolysin, 10 to 18 in placebo), so the claim cannot be verified in either direction.
The paper states no sample-size or power calculation, only that the previous study's sample 'was not large enough'. With no stated effect size, alpha or target power there is nothing to reproduce.

No supplementary files accompany the paper in the provided directory, and data are offered only 'from the corresponding author upon reasonable request', so no raw-data duplication analysis was possible.

not_checked.location: Table 2, exact p-values for the six comparisons this review did not individually recompute in stage 2
not_checked.reason: The sweep recomputed all nine and reported the six unstarred non-significant cells at p = 0.12 to 0.75; this review independently re-verified three of the nine (the two starred cells and the disputed ΔFMA-LL cell) plus ΔFMA-T T0–T1. The remaining five rest on the sweep's computation rather than a stage-2 recheck.

limitations: Figures were NOT read as images in this review. Figure captions were read as text, and the sweep recorded figure metadata from those captions, but no chart was digitised and no value was read off any plot. This matters concretely here: Figure 1 is the CONSORT flowchart, and its box labels — which would carry the per-arm randomised split needed to settle the safety-denominator contradiction — are not in the PDF text layer and were not recovered.

This system reads one paper and reaches no network. Two questions a reader needs in order to weight the Table 2 asterisk finding are outside its reach entirely: whether similar marking or transcription discrepancies appear in the authors' other publications, and how the reported effect sizes and baseline imbalances compare with other Cerebrolysin trials or with the two parent trials (NCT01996761, NCT02768571) reported separately. The interpretation is therefore partly ours and partly the reader's.

The multiplicity tool failed to parse its inputs on every attempt across both stages, returning n_tests = 0. No hand-computed substitute was made, so the report contains no statement about how many of the paper's significant results survive correction. That is a gap in this review, not a finding about the paper.

Three Table 1 p-value findings rest on an assumption this review supplied — that Table 1 was analysed with independent t-tests — because the paper does not state which test was used. They are graded and worded accordingly and none of them is the headline.

statcheck recovered zero statistics because the journal typesets degrees of freedom as subscripts ('F2,107 = 3.202' rather than the APA 'F(2, 107) = 3.202'), which its patterns do not match. All three F-tests were instead verified directly, so no NHST result went unchecked on that account.

Table 1 and Table 2 values cited here were re-read at source from the XML grid in this stage; the sweep separately reconciled Table 1 against the PDF text layer with zero disagreeing cells, and no table was flagged alignment_uncertain or image_only. The extraction is therefore unusually well established for this paper.

questions_for_authors.question: Table 2's footnote reads "* p < 0.05 compared with the placebo group", but the ΔFMA-LL T0–T1 cell (Cerebrolysin 3.3 ± 5.0, n = 59; placebo 5.6 ± 6.0, n = 51) carries no asterisk, while recalculation from those values gives p = 0.031 (pooled) or p = 0.033 (Welch). Could you confirm the p-value for that comparison, and whether every cell in Table 2 was tested or only the T1–T2 comparisons discussed in the text?
questions_for_authors.why: Settles whether a significant result favouring placebo was tested and left unmarked, or never tested, and whether the footnote describes the table accurately.

questions_for_authors.question: Section 2.5 states that the Bonferroni correction was used for multiple comparisons. Which families of tests was it applied to, and what corrected threshold resulted? Table 3 marks eight interactions significant at raw p-values of 0.0091 to 0.0449, which appear to be judged against 0.05.
questions_for_authors.why: Determines whether the imaging results underpinning the title's neuroprotection claim survive the correction the paper says it applied; the multiplicity tool could not be run.

questions_for_authors.question: In Results 3.4, the infusion-completion percentages (96.7% and 87.9%) resolve to denominators of 61 and 58, summing to the stated safety population of 119, whereas the adverse-event percentages (8.1% and 8.3%) resolve to 62 and 60, summing to 122. Could you confirm the per-arm denominators used for the adverse-event rates?
questions_for_authors.why: Resolves an arithmetic contradiction in the safety paragraph and clarifies whether adverse events were computed on the randomised or the treated population.

questions_for_authors.question: Which statistical test produced the p-values in Table 1? Under an independent t-test the printed means and SDs give achievable p-ranges of [0.248, 0.297] for age (reported 0.246), [0.894, 1.0] for NIHSS (reported 0.882) and [0.085, 0.095] for lesion volume (reported 0.117), while the MMSE, FMA-T, FMA-UL and FMA-LL rows reproduce exactly.
questions_for_authors.why: A rank-based test for the skewed and ordinal rows would explain all three discrepancies; the paper does not name the test.

questions_for_authors.question: Results 3.1 states that 174 patients were screened and 122 randomised after 54 exclusions, but 122 + 54 = 176. Should the screening total read 176, or are two patients accounted for elsewhere?
questions_for_authors.why: Reconciles the only participant-flow sum in the paper that does not balance.

questions_for_authors.question: Section 2.1 reads "Inclusion and exclusion criteria for the second trial (NCT02768571) were the same as those used in the first trial (NCT02768571)", giving the same registry identifier for both trials. Should the second instance read NCT01996761?
questions_for_authors.why: This sentence establishes which trial's eligibility criteria, including the FMA-T 0–49 entry restriction defining the population, the pooled dataset was built on.

questions_for_authors.question: Section 2.5 states that "the paired t-test was performed to analyze significant changes from T2 to T1 in participants' imaging measures", but Section 2.1 states that DTI and rs-fMRI were acquired at T0 and T2 only, and Table 3 reports T0 versus T2. Can you confirm that the analysis compared T0 with T2?
questions_for_authors.why: Establishes whether this is a description error in the Methods or a discrepancy in what was analysed.

questions_for_authors.question: The data availability statement offers data "from the corresponding author upon reasonable request". For a pooled secondary analysis of two registered trials (NCT01996761, NCT02768571), would the de-identified participant-level FMA and imaging summary data be deposited in a repository with an accession or DOI?
questions_for_authors.why: Several findings here — the Table 2 marking, the Table 1 test choice, the safety denominators — would be settled immediately by the analysis dataset.

report_markdown:
This is a pooled secondary analysis of two phase IV randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trials of Cerebrolysin added to a standardised rehabilitation programme in subacute ischaemic stroke patients with severe motor impairment. 110 patients form the full analysis set (Cerebrolysin 59, placebo 51), with per-protocol imaging subsets of 92 for diffusion tensor imaging and 81 for resting-state fMRI. The primary outcome is the pattern of total Fugl-Meyer Assessment scores across three timepoints; the paper reports a significant time-by-group interaction and concludes that Cerebrolysin enhances motor recovery and preserves the motor network.

**What verifies.** A good deal, and it should count. The primary outcome reconciles exactly: F(2,107) = 3.202 converts to p = 0.0446 against a reported 0.045, and the degrees of freedom are coherent for a two-group, three-timepoint design at N = 110. Both non-significant limb interactions reconcile exactly too. All three categorical baseline comparisons reconcile, the motor-evoked-potential row matching Fisher's exact test rather than Pearson, which is a legitimate convention at those cell sizes. Both reported Cohen's d values recompute from the printed means and SDs (0.47 reported against 0.461; 0.44 against 0.434) and sit in the ordinary range for a clinical trial. The strongest positive result is the resting-state fMRI block: all eight paired tests report exact four-decimal p-values alongside both timepoint means, SDs and known group sizes, which lets the hidden pre-post correlation be recovered — every one falls in [0.26, 0.67], exactly where ninety-day test-retest reliability of connectivity measures should sit. Thirty-two of thirty-three participant-flow and table sums reconcile, including the non-trivial ones: upper-limb plus lower-limb scores add to the total in both arms, and Table 2's change scores are additive both across components and across time intervals. A duplication scan over 2,274 cross-table comparisons found no identical mean/SD pair anywhere. This is what a carefully computed paper looks like, and the anomalies below sit inside it rather than replacing it.

**How to read the baseline table.** The omnibus baseline-similarity tests were correctly refused, not skipped: the trial states block randomisation of size 4 stratified by clinical centre, which forces balance by construction and would be read by those tests as suspicious uniformity against a properly randomised trial. Table 1's motor rows are also mutually predictive by definition. So there is no Carlisle-style signature here, and none is claimed. The opposite pattern deserves attention instead. Four baseline p-values cluster between 0.085 and 0.117, and all four lean the same way: the Cerebrolysin arm started with 4.6 more Fugl-Meyer points and 26 cm³ less infarct. The paper reports this as "no significant differences" and adjusts for none of it, while its own Discussion states that acute motor function is the strongest predictor of three-month outcome. Non-significant is not absent, and with no confidence interval anywhere in the paper there is no way to bound how much of the treatment effect the head start could carry.

**Context for the marking asymmetry.** The study was funded by EVER Neuro Pharma GmbH, the manufacturer of Cerebrolysin, alongside a Korean government grant; the authors declare no conflict of interest. Many journals treat funding and competing interests as separate disclosures, so this is not in itself irregular. It is, however, the relevant background for the finding that the single Table 2 comparison favouring placebo is the single significant comparison left unstarred. The modal innocent explanation is stated in that finding and is genuinely the likeliest one — authors commonly test only the contrasts they intend to discuss, and the text discusses only the T1–T2 comparisons — but the footnote as written promises a threshold the table does not apply uniformly.

**Manuscript preparation.** Several defects point the same way: an imaging comparison described in the Methods between timepoints that were never both scanned, the same registry number given for both pooled trials, a data availability statement printed twice, a placebo denominator of 52 where every other mention says 51, a screening total two short, and a Discussion sentence ("the manuscript provides an overly positive impression of the use of pharmacotherapies in stroke rehabilitation") that reads more like an unaddressed reviewer comment than authorial prose. Individually each is trivial. Together they indicate the manuscript was not closely proofread, which is the most economical explanation for the two arithmetic impossibilities and is worth weighing before any less charitable reading.

The efficacy signal here is real but thin — a primary interaction at p = 0.045, uncorrected, on a sample whose arms differed at baseline in the treatment's favour — and the neuroprotection claim rests on eight borderline imaging interactions whose survival under the paper's own stated correction could not be established. The paper's numbers are largely internally coherent; what is unresolved is which tests produced several of them, and how much of the headline result survives its own multiplicity. I would want the analysis dataset and a clarification of Table 2's markings before relying on the efficacy conclusion.
